abstract.text:
A new notion of equilibrium, which we call strong equilibrium, is introduced for time-inconsistent stopping problems in continuous time. Compared to the existing notions introduced
in (Huang & Nguyen-Huu, 2018) and (Christensen & Lindensjö, 2018), which in this paper are
called mild equilibrium and weak equilibrium respectively, a strong equilibrium captures the idea
of subgame perfect Nash equilibrium more accurately. When the state process is a continuoustime Markov chain and the discount function is log sub-additive, we show that an optimal mild
equilibrium is always a strong equilibrium. Moreover, we provide a new iteration method that can
directly construct an optimal mild equilibrium and thus also prove its existence.

sections.summary: Introduces time-inconsistent optimal stopping under non-exponential discounting and reviews the existing mild and weak equilibrium notions. The problem is framed as consistent planning, i.e. a subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium. Mild equilibrium only checks continuation values for states outside the stopping region; weak equilibrium adds a first-order deviation condition. The paper argues both notions are economically inadequate in continuous time, especially because return times may be zero and first-order limits may hide profitable deviations.
sections.title: Time-Inconsistency and Existing Equilibrium Notions

source_span.end_text: This paper provides very novel and conceptual contributions in the topic of time-inconsistent stopping.

sections.summary: Defines strong equilibrium, which requires that at every stopping state there be no profitable continuation deviation for all sufficiently small positive delays. This is presented as a more accurate formulation of subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium than mild or weak equilibrium. The unit also states the paper’s main contributions: proving optimal mild equilibria are strong, constructing an optimal mild equilibrium by iteration, and mapping the containment relations among mild, weak, strong, and optimal mild equilibria. Applications to finance and economics are previewed.

sections.summary: Contains the technical proof that an optimal mild equilibrium is strong. Proposition 2.1 converts the weak equilibrium first-order condition into an explicit inequality. Corollary 2.1 shows that a mild equilibrium satisfying a strict version of that inequality is strong. Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2 compare values after removing a state and establish key inequalities used to rule out profitable continuation at stopping states. The proof splits singleton and multi-state cases and concludes strong equilibrium.

sections.summary: Develops an infinite-state American-option example under hyperbolic discounting. The underlying stock Y takes values ui, and the payoff is X = f(Y) = (K − y)+. Lemma 3.1 characterizes S1 in terms of continuation values. Proposition 3.2 identifies the iteration limit S∞ as a threshold set {ui : i ≤ n0}, where n0 is determined by the payoff ratio and a discount-dependent constant α1. The iteration terminates in finitely many steps.

sections.summary: Discusses how non-standard discounting affects option exercise timing. It defines the pre-commitment optimal stopping problem with value U(y) and its optimal stopping time τ*. Proposition 3.3 shows that the equilibrium stopping time τS∞ is earlier than or equal to τ* under a generic non-integer condition. The interpretation is that a sophisticated agent who accounts for future preference changes will exercise the American put option sooner than a pre-committed agent would.

sections.summary: Uses a two-state continuous-time Markov chain to show exact containment relations among equilibrium concepts. The set {a, b} is always mild, while {a} is mild only under a value condition. Cases distinguish when equilibria are optimal mild, weak, strong, or only weak. A second-order expansion yields conditions under which {a, b} is weak but not strong. Hyperbolic discounting makes weak equilibrium strong in this two-state setting, while a power discount function can produce a weak-but-not-strong equilibrium.

sections.summary: Introduces time-inconsistent optimal stopping under non-exponential discounting and reviews the existing mild and weak equilibrium notions. The problem is framed as consistent planning, i.e. a subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium. Mild equilibrium only checks continuation values for states outside the stopping region; weak equilibrium adds a first-order deviation condition. The paper argues both notions are economically inadequate in continuous time, especially because return times may be zero and first-order limits may hide profitable deviations.

sections.summary: Defines strong equilibrium, which requires that at every stopping state there be no profitable continuation deviation for all sufficiently small positive delays. This is presented as a more accurate formulation of subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium than mild or weak equilibrium. The unit also states the paper’s main contributions: proving optimal mild equilibria are strong, constructing an optimal mild equilibrium by iteration, and mapping the containment relations among mild, weak, strong, and optimal mild equilibria. Applications to finance and economics are previewed.

sections.summary: Discusses how non-standard discounting affects option exercise timing. It defines the pre-commitment optimal stopping problem with value U(y) and its optimal stopping time τ*. Proposition 3.3 shows that the equilibrium stopping time τS∞ is earlier than or equal to τ* under a generic non-integer condition. The interpretation is that a sophisticated agent who accounts for future preference changes will exercise the American put option sooner than a pre-committed agent would.

sections.summary: Uses a two-state continuous-time Markov chain to show exact containment relations among equilibrium concepts. The set {a, b} is always mild, while {a} is mild only under a value condition. Cases distinguish when equilibria are optimal mild, weak, strong, or only weak. A second-order expansion yields conditions under which {a, b} is weak but not strong. Hyperbolic discounting makes weak equilibrium strong in this two-state setting, while a power discount function can produce a weak-but-not-strong equilibrium.
